title: Virtual memory and paging
scopeHtml: Scope: virtual address spaces, page tables, TLB, page faults, page replacement and thrashing, huge pages, segfaults and memory debugging.

notes.title: Why virtual memory
notes.html:
Virtual memory gives every process the illusion of its own huge, private, contiguous memory, while the OS maps those virtual addresses onto limited, shared physical RAM.

What it buys:

  1. Isolation: process A cannot even name process B's memory.
  2. Simplicity: every program is compiled assuming the same layout (code low, heap grows up, stack grows down).
  3. More than RAM: pages not in use can live on disk or not exist yet.
  4. Sharing: the same physical page of libc can be mapped into 500 processes.
  5. Lazy work: memory is only really allocated when touched.

Address layout of a 64-bit Linux process (simplified):

high  kernel space (not accessible in user mode)
      stack            (grows down)
      mmap region      (shared libs, mmap files, big mallocs)
      heap             (grows up via brk)
      data / bss       (globals)
low   text            (code)
cat /proc/<pid>/maps | head -5
00400000-00452000 r-xp 00000000 08:01 131 /usr/bin/myapp       # code
7f3a1c000000-7f3a1c021000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0                 # heap/anon
7ffd4a2e0000-7ffd4a301000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0 [stack]

Worked example. A 64-bit machine with 16 GB RAM can run 100 JVMs each reserving a 4 GB heap (-Xmx4g) because virtual reservations are not physical use. Only touched pages cost RAM. Hence VSZ in ps can be enormous while RSS is small.

Industry examples. Android relies on it: Zygote forked apps share the framework's pages. Databases mmap data files; JVM reserves its heap address range at startup.

Everyday analogy. A hotel guest holds a room number (virtual) printed on the key; the front desk (MMU and OS) decides which real room that maps to, and different guests' "room 101" are different rooms.

Common interview traps.

  • Equating virtual size (VSZ) with memory use. Look at RSS or PSS.
  • Saying virtual memory "is" swap. Swap is one optional piece.

notes.title: Paging and page tables
notes.html:
Memory is cut into fixed-size pages (4 KB on x86 and most ARM Linux). Virtual pages map to physical frames of the same size through a page table. No external fragmentation, any page can go in any frame.

Virtual address = page number + offset. Example with 4 KB pages: address 0x7F3A1C002ABC has offset 0xABC (low 12 bits) and the rest is the virtual page number, looked up in the page table to get a frame number; offset is copied unchanged.

A flat table for 48-bit addresses would need 2^36 entries x 8 B = 512 GB per process, so x86-64 uses a 4-level radix tree: PGD, PUD, PMD, PTE, each a 4 KB table of 512 entries (9 bits per level). Only the parts in use exist. (5-level paging exists for 57-bit addresses.)

Each page-table entry (PTE) holds: frame number, present bit, read/write, user/supervisor, accessed, dirty, no-execute (NX) bits. These bits drive protection, swapping and page reclaim.

Worked example. A process touching 1 GB (262,144 pages) needs 262,144 x 8 B = 2 MB of PTEs. 1000 such processes use 2 GB just for page tables. Forking a 20 GB Redis copies about 40 MB of tables (see the processes note).

$ grep -E 'PageTables|VmPTE' /proc/meminfo /proc/<pid>/status
PageTables:       184320 kB
VmPTE:             2048 kB

Decision gravity. Page size is a hardware/OS config: 4 KB is the compromise between fragmentation and table size. Larger pages cut table size and TLB misses but waste memory for small allocations; it's changeable per mapping (huge pages) but not globally cheaply.

Everyday analogy. A book index: the page number tells you which shelf (frame), and the line within the page stays the same.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting multilevel tables exist to save memory.
  • Thinking one page table is shared; each process has its own.

notes.title: TLB
notes.html:
The TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer) is a tiny, very fast cache of recent virtual to physical translations inside the CPU. Without it each memory access would take up to 4 extra memory reads for the page walk.

Numbers (typical, varies by CPU): L1 dTLB about 64 entries, L2 TLB about 1,500 to 2,000. With 4 KB pages 1,536 entries cover only 6 MB. A TLB hit adds about 1 cycle; a miss triggers a hardware page walk of roughly tens to hundreds of cycles depending on cache hits.

Hit ratio is usually 99%+ for programs with locality, which is why paging is affordable; random access across huge data (large hash tables, database buffer pools) misses often.

TLB and context switches:

  • Switching address space (process switch) would invalidate the TLB; PCID/ASID tags let entries of several processes coexist.
  • Changing a mapping on one core requires a TLB shootdown: an inter-processor interrupt to flush entries on other cores. munmap/mprotect heavy multi-threaded programs suffer (visible as TLB: in /proc/interrupts).
  • KPTI (Meltdown fix) makes every syscall switch tables, costing TLB misses unless PCID is used.
perf stat -e dTLB-load-misses,dTLB-loads ./app   # miss ratio
grep TLB /proc/interrupts                         # shootdown counts

Worked example. A 100 GB in-memory index with 4 KB pages needs 26 million translations; the TLB holds 1.5 thousand, so random lookups nearly always miss. Moving to 2 MB huge pages shrinks that to 51,200 translations, and DB vendors report 5% to 30% speedups from this (confirm for your workload).

Everyday analogy. Keeping the 20 phone numbers you call most on a sticky note instead of searching the directory every time.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the TLB caches data. It caches translations.
  • Forgetting shootdown cost when discussing munmap in threads.

notes.title: Page faults
notes.html:
A page fault happens when a program touches a virtual page that is not currently mapped to a usable frame. The CPU traps to the kernel, which fixes it or kills the process.

Types:

  • Minor (soft): page is in RAM but not mapped for this process (first touch of zero page, COW, file page in the page cache). Cost about 0.5 to 2 microseconds.
  • Major (hard): data must be read from disk (swap-in, or first read of an mmapped file not in cache). Cost 0.1 ms on SSD to 10 ms on HDD, 10,000x worse.
  • Invalid: access to an unmapped address or wrong permission; delivered as SIGSEGV.

Handler logic: find the VMA (virtual memory area) covering the address; if none or wrong permission, SIGSEGV; otherwise allocate a frame, fill it (zeros, file read, swap read, COW copy), update PTE, restart the instruction.

Demand paging: malloc(1 GB) costs almost nothing; each 4 KB gets a frame at first touch via a minor fault. Zeroing a big array then reveals the real cost.

$ /usr/bin/time -v ./app
    Major (requiring I/O) page faults: 3
    Minor (reclaiming a frame) page faults: 412380
$ pidstat -r 1
 PID   minflt/s  majflt/s  VSZ     RSS   %MEM
 4410   3200.00      0.00  4.1g    900m  5.6

Production reading: rising majflt/s means the working set no longer fits in RAM or the page cache is thrashed (latency spikes, vmstat shows si/so or high bi). High minflt is usually normal allocation churn; a JVM started with -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch pays all faults up front for stable latency.

Industry examples. Redis latency docs warn that swapping/major faults cause multi-second pauses; Android kills background processes before they thrash. Mmap-based databases (LMDB, early MongoDB) rely on faults for I/O, which made latency less predictable than explicit buffer pools.

Everyday analogy. Opening a reference book that is in the library basement. Minor: someone already put it on a nearby shelf. Major: staff must fetch it from storage, you wait.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating every page fault as an error.
  • Mixing up minor/major fault costs.
  • Forgetting that the instruction is restarted after the fault.

notes.title: Page replacement
notes.html:
When RAM is full, the kernel must pick a page to evict, and writes it out first if dirty. Goal: evict the page least likely to be needed soon.

Classic algorithms:

  • OPT (Belady): evict the page used furthest in the future. Optimal, impossible, a benchmark.
  • FIFO: simple but suffers Belady's anomaly (more frames can cause more faults).
  • LRU: evict least recently used; good, but exact tracking is expensive.
  • Clock (second chance): pages in a circle with an accessed bit; hand sweeps, clearing bits, evicting the first page whose bit is 0. Cheap approximation of LRU.

Linux uses split active and inactive LRU lists for anonymous and file pages (newer kernels add multi-generational LRU, MGLRU, 6.1+). A page gets promoted when referenced twice; kswapd reclaims in the background when free memory falls under the low watermark, and direct reclaim stalls the allocating process when it falls under min watermark. Clean file pages are cheap to drop (re-readable); anonymous pages need swap. vm.swappiness (0 to 100, default 60) biases between swapping anonymous pages and dropping file cache.

Thrashing: working set bigger than RAM, so the system spends its time swapping and doing no work. Signs: vmstat si/so non-zero continuously, high wa, kswapd at 100% CPU in top, PSI memory full avg10 greater than 0.

$ vmstat 1
 r b   swpd   free  buff cache   si   so   bi   bo
 3 4 2201344  31244  1204 80200 5200 7400 5300 7600   <- thrashing

Worked example. Bubble sort on a 20 GB array with 16 GB RAM: LRU evicts the page just about to be reused in a sequential loop (the classic LRU bad case); every pass re-reads the data from disk.

Decision gravity. Configuring swap (none, small, zram) is reversible at runtime; database hosts often use swappiness=1 and Kubernetes historically required swap off (newer versions allow it).

Everyday analogy. A small desk: when it fills, you put the papers you touched least recently back in the cabinet.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing LRU is optimal (OPT is).
  • Reading "free" memory as the real availability; Linux uses spare RAM for cache. Use available in free -m.

notes.title: Huge pages
notes.html:
Huge pages use 2 MB (or 1 GB) pages instead of 4 KB, so fewer TLB entries and fewer page table levels cover the same memory.

Two kinds on Linux:

  • Explicit hugetlbfs pages: reserved up front (vm.nr_hugepages=2048 gives 4 GB), applications ask via mmap(MAP_HUGETLB). Predictable, never swapped. Used by Oracle, PostgreSQL (huge_pages = try), DPDK, JVM -XX:+UseLargePages.
  • Transparent Huge Pages (THP): the kernel promotes ranges automatically (khugepaged). Convenient but can cause latency spikes (compaction stalls, big COW copies, memory bloat). cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled shows [always] madvise never.

Guidance: Redis, MongoDB, and many latency-sensitive stores say set THP to madvise or never. Large DBs with a big shared buffer often benefit from explicit huge pages.

grep -i huge /proc/meminfo
HugePages_Total:    2048
HugePages_Free:     2048
Hugepagesize:       2048 kB
AnonHugePages:   4194304 kB
echo madvise > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled

Worked example. PostgreSQL shared_buffers = 32 GB with 4 KB pages: 8.4 million PTEs per backend (about 64 MB of page tables per connection, times 300 connections is ~19 GB wasted). With 2 MB huge pages the tables shrink by 512x. This is the textbook reason to set huge_pages = on.

Everyday analogy. Selling pencils by the box of 100 instead of one at a time: fewer line items to track, but you may end up with unused pencils.

Common interview traps.

  • Enabling THP everywhere because it "improves performance" without measuring tail latency.
  • Forgetting explicit huge pages must be reserved and are not available to normal allocations.

notes.title: Segmentation faults and debugging memory
notes.html:
A segmentation fault (SIGSEGV) is the invalid page fault: the process touched memory it has no right to. Typical causes: null or dangling pointer, buffer overflow into an unmapped page, stack overflow (deep recursion hits the guard page, 8 MB limit via ulimit -s), writing to read-only code or string literals.

Tools:

ulimit -c unlimited                 # enable core dumps
gdb ./app core                      # then: bt
valgrind --tool=memcheck ./app      # finds invalid access, leaks (slow, 20x)
gcc -fsanitize=address -g app.c     # AddressSanitizer, ~2x slowdown
dmesg | tail                        # "app[4410]: segfault at 0 ip ... error 4"

Memory accounting commands:

$ pmap -x <pid> | tail -3
total kB         4218120  912340  901220
$ free -m
              total  used  free  shared  buff/cache  available
Mem:          15984  6120   310     210        9553       9400
$ cat /proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup   # Rss, Pss, Shared, Private, Swap

Java and Android analogue: StackOverflowError, OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space vs native OOM (kernel kills JVM when total, including metaspace, thread stacks and direct buffers, exceeds RAM or cgroup limit).

Everyday analogy. Walking into a room with a "staff only" or nonexistent door; security (the kernel) escorts you out.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling any crash a segfault; Java never segfaults from application code (JNI can).
  • Looking at VSZ instead of RSS or PSS when judging leaks.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Virtual memory = private per-process address space mapped onto shared physical RAM: isolation, simplicity, sharing, lazy allocation.
  • Pages are 4 KB; x86-64 uses a 4-level page table walk; PTE bits (present, dirty, accessed, NX) drive everything.
  • The TLB caches translations (covering a few MB with 4 KB pages); misses cost a page walk; shootdowns hurt multi-threaded munmap.
  • Page faults: minor (about microseconds), major (disk, ms), invalid (SIGSEGV). Demand paging makes allocation lazy.
  • Replacement: OPT is ideal, LRU approximated by clock and Linux active/inactive lists; kswapd, watermarks, swappiness; thrashing shows as swap traffic plus high wa and PSI memory.
  • Huge pages cut TLB and page-table overhead (Postgres, JVM, DPDK) but THP can cause latency spikes (Redis, MongoDB).
  • Debug with /proc/<pid>/maps|smaps_rollup, pidstat -r, vmstat, perf stat, gdb, ASan.

questions.promptHtml: What is virtual memory and why do operating systems use it? Why can ps show 8 GB VSZ for a process using 300 MB?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Foundation question; shows whether you can separate address space from physical memory use.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Virtual memory gives each process its own private, contiguous-looking address space, and the MMU plus the OS map those virtual addresses to physical RAM frames. It gives isolation, a uniform layout for every program, sharing of common pages (like libc), lazy allocation, and the ability to use more memory than RAM. VSZ counts address space that is reserved or mapped; RSS counts only pages actually resident in RAM, so a process can reserve 8 GB and touch 300 MB.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Every memory access uses a virtual address; hardware translates it via page tables to a physical frame. Memory is committed lazily: malloc(1 GB) or mmap creates a mapping (a VMA) but no frames; a frame is assigned on first touch through a page fault.

high  kernel space
      stack          (grows down)
      mmap region    (shared libs, file maps, big mallocs)
      heap           (brk, grows up)
      data / bss
low   text (code)

Why VSZ lies: JVMs reserve the whole -Xmx range up front; thread stacks reserve 8 MB virtual each; shared libraries are counted fully in every process although they share physical pages. Better measures: RSS, and PSS (shared pages divided among sharers) from /proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup.

ps -o pid,vsz,rss,cmd -p 4410
grep -E 'Rss|Pss|Swap' /proc/4410/smaps_rollup

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating VSZ with memory use and "fixing" a non-problem.
  • Saying virtual memory means swap. Swap is one optional part.
  • Summing RSS across processes to get the total (shared pages are double counted).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How can 100 JVMs with -Xmx4g run on a 16 GB box? -> Reservations are virtual; only touched pages use RAM, though real usage must still fit.
  2. What gives sharing between processes? -> Page tables of different processes pointing to the same frame (libc text, file-backed mmaps, COW after fork).
  3. What protects process A from B? -> Separate page tables; B has no PTE for A's memory, and the user/supervisor and NX bits restrict access.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "virtual memory lets you use more memory than RAM". Senior: isolation and lazy commit are the main points; picks RSS/PSS vs VSZ correctly and ties it to overcommit and OOM behaviour.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An alert on VSZ paged on-call nightly for a Java service until the team switched it to working-set (RSS) based alerts.

questions.promptHtml: What is a page fault? Distinguish minor, major and invalid faults and say which should worry you.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Page faults are the root of many latency and crash symptoms; interviewers want the cost model.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A page fault is a CPU trap when a process touches a virtual page that is not currently mapped to a usable frame. A minor fault is resolved without disk I/O (first touch of zero page, copy-on-write, a file page already in cache) and costs about a microsecond. A major fault needs disk I/O (swap-in or cold mmapped file) and costs 0.1 ms on SSD to ms on HDD. An invalid fault is a bad address or permission violation and becomes SIGSEGV. Major faults are the ones to worry about.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Handler logic: find the VMA for the address; none or wrong permissions means SIGSEGV; otherwise allocate or locate a frame, fill it (zeros, file read, swap read, COW copy), update the PTE, and restart the instruction.

access -> trap -> find VMA -> [no VMA / bad perms: SIGSEGV]
                           -> allocate/read frame -> set PTE -> retry instruction

Demand paging means allocation costs are paid at first touch, so a big memset after malloc shows the real cost. Watch with:

$ pidstat -r 1
 PID   minflt/s  majflt/s  VSZ    RSS
 4410   3200.00      0.00  4.1g   900m
$ /usr/bin/time -v ./app    # Major (requiring I/O) page faults: 3

Rising majflt/s signals working set exceeding RAM or a cold cache.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating every page fault as an error; most are normal.
  • Mixing up the costs (a major fault is roughly 10,000x a minor).
  • Forgetting the faulting instruction is re-executed after the fix.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is malloc(1GB) instant? -> Only a VMA is created; frames arrive on touch.
  2. Which fault happens on the first write after fork? -> A minor COW fault: the kernel copies the page.
  3. How do you remove fault jitter at JVM start? -> -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch and optionally huge pages.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "access to memory not in RAM". Senior gives the three classes, the handler algorithm, the cost gap, and ties major faults to swap, cold mmap and tail latency.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A search node's p99 tripled after restart because mmapped index pages were cold; pre-reading the files removed the major-fault storm.

questions.promptHtml: What is the TLB, and why does a TLB miss cost more than an ordinary cache miss?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks hardware-aware reasoning about paging overhead, a basis for huge-page questions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The TLB is a small, fast cache inside the CPU of recent virtual-to-physical translations. Without it every memory access would first walk the multi-level page table, up to 4 extra memory reads on x86-64. A hit adds about a cycle. On a miss, hardware walks the page table, which can cost tens to hundreds of cycles, and the data access cannot start until the translation finishes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Typical sizes: L1 dTLB around 64 entries, L2 TLB around 1,500 to 2,000 (varies by CPU). With 4 KB pages, 1,536 entries cover only about 6 MB. Programs with good locality hit 99%+; random access over large data (a big hash table, DB buffer pool) misses constantly.

VA -> TLB hit ------------------------> PA -> cache/RAM
VA -> TLB miss -> page walk (PGD,PUD,PMD,PTE) -> fill TLB -> PA

Related costs:

  • Context switch between processes needs ASID/PCID tags or a flush.
  • Changing a mapping (munmap, mprotect) needs a TLB shootdown: an IPI to other cores that may hold the entry.
  • KPTI (Meltdown mitigation) switches tables at each syscall.
perf stat -e dTLB-loads,dTLB-load-misses ./app
grep TLB /proc/interrupts

A miss is worse than a normal cache miss because it is serial: translation first, then the data access, and the page-table entries themselves may miss in cache too.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying the TLB caches data; it caches translations.
  • Ignoring multi-core shootdowns when discussing munmap.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do huge pages help? -> One entry covers 2 MB, so the same TLB reaches 512x more memory.
  2. Does a process switch always flush the TLB? -> Not with PCID/ASID tagging.
  3. What workload suffers most? -> Random access over tens of GB: hash joins, in-memory indexes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "cache for page table". Senior: reach in MB, miss penalty structure, shootdown IPIs, PCID, and huge pages as the remedy with a measured miss rate.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 120 GB in-memory index gained double-digit percent throughput from huge pages purely through fewer dTLB misses (verify with perf stat on your hardware).

questions.contextHtml:
At 09:00 a 16 GB analytics API node (JVM heap 6 GB, plus a Redis cache and a batch job added yesterday) goes from p99 120 ms to 9 s. CPU shows 5% user, 40% iowait. Disk is a network SSD.

$ vmstat 1
 r b   swpd    free  buff cache   si    so    bi    bo
 1 6 3201344   31244  1204 80200 5200  7400  5300  7600
 0 7 3405120   29110  1180 79100 6100  8100  6200  8000
$ cat /proc/pressure/memory
some avg10=71.20  full avg10=48.30
$ top
  PID USER  %CPU COMMAND
   45 root  98.7 kswapd0

A teammate says "iowait is high so the disk is slow; upgrade the disk." Another says "free is only 30 MB, add a swap file." The batch job's RSS is 7 GB.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Upgrading the disk or adding swap; reads free as the problem and ignores si/so and PSI.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed yesterday (the batch job)? Is there a cgroup limit? Swap size and swappiness? Has this node seen RSS growth over time?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop or kill -STOP the batch job to free 7 GB; if needed echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/swappiness is not an immediate cure; shed traffic from the node at the LB.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) working set larger than RAM so the node is thrashing (continuous si/so 5-8 MB/s, PSI full 48%); (b) slow disk; (c) memory leak in JVM; (d) page cache starvation. si/so nonzero while bi/bo mirror them and kswapd at 98% points at (a).
  4. How I'd verify: smem -rtk for PSS ranking; grep VmSwap per process to see whose pages are swapped; pidstat -r for majflt/s; compare memory demand sums: 6 GB heap + JVM overhead + Redis + 7 GB batch exceeds 16 GB.
  5. Root cause: Total demand exceeds RAM. The kernel evicts the pages of the hot API (including JVM heap and code) to swap and brings them back on the next touch; each major fault costs ms, so requests stall. kswapd burns CPU scanning and direct reclaim stalls allocators. Low free was never the issue; the continuous swap traffic and PSI full were.
  6. Fix: Short term: stop the batch job and swapoff -a && swapon -a only after RSS drops, to return pages. Long term: put the batch job on its own node or cgroup with memory.max, size heap/Redis explicitly, and set Redis maxmemory.
  7. Prevention: Alert on si/so > 1 MB/s for 5 min and PSI memory full; memory budget in design review; separate batch from latency-sensitive tiers.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not more swap (turns a crash into a slow death); not disk upgrade; not drop_caches (masks and hurts). Swappiness tuning helps only at the margin.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is PSI better than free? -> It measures time stalled waiting for memory.
  • What if there is no swap? -> Then thrashing shows as page cache eviction and major faults on file pages (code), then OOM.
  • Would zram help? -> Buys time with 2-3x compression but still not a fix when demand doubles RAM.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "just add a nightly report job to the API host" change caused a Monday-morning brownout. The fix took five minutes (move the job); the diagnosis took two hours because everyone stared at free.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Upgrades disk or adds swap; reads free literally.
  • Hire: Recognises thrashing from si/so, kswapd, PSI, and removes the memory hog.
  • Strong hire: Quantifies demand vs RAM, isolates workloads with cgroups, adds PSI alerting.

questions.promptHtml: Why does x86-64 use a 4-level page table instead of a flat one, and how much memory do page tables take for a process with 1 GB resident?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests first-principles sizing and whether you know page tables cost real RAM.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A flat table for a 48-bit space with 4 KB pages needs 2^36 entries x 8 bytes = 512 GB per process, which is absurd. A radix tree of four levels (PGD, PUD, PMD, PTE), each a 4 KB table of 512 entries, only allocates the pieces in use. For 1 GB resident, that is 262,144 pages x 8 bytes = 2 MB of leaf PTEs plus a few KB of upper levels.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A virtual address splits into 9+9+9+9 bits of table indexes plus a 12-bit page offset. Each PTE holds frame number and flags: present, read/write, user/supervisor, accessed, dirty, NX. The offset is copied unchanged.

48-bit VA: [PGD 9][PUD 9][PMD 9][PTE 9][offset 12]
CR3 -> PGD -> PUD -> PMD -> PTE -> frame

Costs:

  • 1000 processes of 1 GB each: 2 GB of page tables. See PageTables: in /proc/meminfo and VmPTE in /proc/<pid>/status.
  • fork copies page tables (not data): a 20 GB Redis copies about 40 MB of PTEs, causing latency spikes.
  • A walk touches up to 4 memory locations, which is why the TLB exists.
  • 5-level paging (57-bit) exists for very large address spaces.

Huge pages stop one level earlier: a 2 MB page is mapped by a PMD entry directly, shrinking the tables 512x.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting multi-level tables exist to save memory, not to be faster.
  • Believing one page table is shared among all processes; each has its own (kernel mappings are shared).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why 512 entries per table? -> 4 KB table / 8-byte entries = 512, so each level indexes 9 bits.
  2. What are the accessed and dirty bits for? -> Page replacement picks cold pages by accessed; dirty tells if write-back is needed.
  3. Why can fork of a big process stall? -> It must copy and write-protect PTEs of every private page (COW setup).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "table maps pages to frames". Senior computes sizes, explains the sparse tree, links PTE overhead to fork latency and huge pages.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Postgres host with 300 connections and 32 GB shared buffers lost many GB to per-backend page tables until huge pages were enabled.

questions.contextHtml:
A small C++ tool crashes with a segmentation fault only on some inputs, and only in release builds. Logs:

$ dmesg | tail -1
tool[4410]: segfault at 7ffd3a2f9000 ip 000055b1c8a0123a sp 00007ffd3a2f9010 error 6 in tool[55b1c8a00000+2000]

Code:

#include <cstring>
#include <cstdio>

char* greeting() { char buf[16]; std::strcpy(buf, "hello"); return buf; }

void deep(int n) { char pad[4096]; pad[0] = (char)n; if (n) deep(n - 1); }

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    char* s = (char*)"hello world";
    s[0] = 'J';                    // (1)
    printf("%s\n", greeting());    // (2)
    deep(argc > 1 ? atoi(argv[1]) : 10);   // (3)
    char name[8]; strcpy(name, argv[1]);   // (4)
}

Run with ulimit -s = 8192 (KB). A teammate says it must be a compiler optimisation bug.
questions.promptHtml: List every memory bug here, say which one produced the logged crash, and how to find these in practice.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Null pointer" or "compiler bug" without distinguishing the four faults or mentioning tools.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which input crashes? Debug vs release difference (stack layout, optimisation)? Compiler flags and whether ASan was tried?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reproduce with the failing input and get a core dump (ulimit -c unlimited) so we do not guess.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) stack overflow through deep recursion (4 KB x N frames > 8 MB at N about 2,000+); (b) write to a string literal (read-only page, error 7); (c) returning a pointer to a local; (d) buffer overflow in name.
  4. How I'd verify: The log says fault address 7ffd3a2f9000, next to the stack pointer 7ffd3a2f9010, with error code 6 (user-mode write to an unmapped/guard page). The fault address is next to sp, so the stack grew into the guard page: stack overflow from deep. gdb tool core then bt shows thousands of deep frames. Build with -fsanitize=address -g to catch the others.
  5. Root cause: Bug (3) is the logged crash: deep(n) uses a 4 KB frame per call, and a large n exhausts the 8 MB stack. Bug (1): string literals live in read-only memory, so writing s[0] faults with a protection error (error 7, SIGSEGV). Bug (2): greeting returns the address of a dead stack frame (undefined behaviour). Bug (4): strcpy into 8 bytes overflows; argv[1] may also be null.
  6. Fix: Use const char* or a char s[] = "..." copy; return std::string; replace deep recursion with a loop or bound the depth; use snprintf/std::string and check argc.
  7. Prevention: Build CI with ASan/UBSan, -Wall -Wextra -Werror, static analysis, fuzzing for input parsing; core dumps enabled in staging.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not raising ulimit -s to hide recursion; not blaming the optimiser before sanitisers have run. ASan is about 2x slower so it belongs in CI, not production; valgrind is about 20x slower.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did only release crash? -> Layout and inlining changed; undefined behaviour often hides in debug builds.
  • How would a Java version of (3) fail? -> StackOverflowError, a managed exception, not a segfault.
  • Can you catch SIGSEGV from a stack overflow? -> Only on an alternate stack (sigaltstack), and recovery is unsafe.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A parser crashed in production on hostile deeply nested JSON; the bug was recursion depth, found only when a core dump and bt showed 40,000 identical frames.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Cannot separate causes; blames compiler.
  • Hire: Identifies stack overflow from the fault address near sp and finds the literal write.
  • Strong hire: Finds all four, uses gdb/ASan, and proposes CI sanitisers and fuzzing.

questions.contextHtml:
A manager asks you: "Our monitoring says each of our 40 Java microservices uses about 6 GB of memory, but the nodes only have 32 GB and each hosts 8 of them, which would be 48 GB. Is this a capacity problem? Do we need bigger nodes? We got an alert at 90% memory on two nodes." You have:

$ ps -o pid,vsz,rss,cmd -C java | head -3
 PID      VSZ      RSS CMD
4410  6291456  1810432 java -Xmx4g -jar orders.jar
4415  6389120  1752064 java -Xmx4g -jar users.jar
$ free -m
        total  used  free  shared  buff/cache  available
Mem:    32000  16400  2100     300       13500      14800
$ grep -E 'Pss|Rss' /proc/4410/smaps_rollup
Rss: 1810432 kB   Pss: 1650000 kB

The alert fires on (total - free) / total.
questions.promptHtml: What do you tell the manager, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Buy bigger nodes" because 8 x 6 GB > 32 GB, or "all is fine" without checking what the alert measures.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does the dashboard's 6 GB represent (VSZ, heap max, container limit)? Are the two alerting nodes behaving differently (swap, OOM kills)? Are containers limited?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed for capacity: the node has 14.8 GB available. Silence/replace the misleading alert, and confirm no OOMKilled in kubectl or dmesg.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the dashboard graphs VSZ, which includes reserved heap and mapped files; (b) the alert counts page cache as used (total - free); (c) a real leak on two nodes; (d) per-node imbalance.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare VSZ 6.0 GB with RSS 1.8 GB / PSS 1.65 GB for each JVM: 8 x 1.8 = 14.4 GB of RSS fits 16.4 GB used; buff/cache 13.5 GB is reclaimable. Check MemAvailable trend and PSI memory on the two nodes, plus dmesg -T | grep -i oom.
  5. Root cause: Two metric mistakes: using virtual size as "memory" and counting reclaimable page cache as used. Virtual reservation is not RAM; the real footprint is about 1.8 GB each.
  6. Fix: Dashboard on working set / RSS (or container working_set_bytes), alert on MemAvailable below 10%, plus PSI memory. Document the request/limit per service: heap max plus metaspace plus threads (about 60-75% rule).
  7. Prevention: Capacity review uses p95 RSS per service, not VSZ; add per-node available panel; set JVM MaxRAMPercentage.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not buying nodes; not lowering -Xmx blindly (JVM RSS will grow toward Xmx under load, so the sizing must allow it: 8 x 4 GB heap plus overhead could still be up to about 40 GB at peak if all heaps fill). So I'd check peak heap usage over a week before concluding it is safe, because Xmx is a ceiling that a busy heap approaches.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if all 8 JVMs reach their Xmx? -> Then 8 x ~4.8 GB = 38 GB, over the node: that is the real risk; limit packing or reduce heaps.
  • Is PSS or RSS better for the sum? -> PSS, as it divides shared pages fairly.
  • What if the alert was right on the two nodes? -> Look at kernel memory (Slab, PageTables) and non-JVM processes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cost-cutting project nearly doubled the node size because a dashboard multiplied VSZ by pod count. Switching the panel to RSS cut the planned spend to nothing.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Takes 6 GB at face value or declares "fine" without evidence.
  • Hire: Separates VSZ from RSS/PSS and fixes the alert to use available memory.
  • Strong hire: Also notes Xmx as a peak ceiling, does worst-case packing math, and proposes capacity process.

questions.promptHtml: Compare OPT, FIFO, LRU and Clock page replacement. What does Linux actually do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Classic CS question; the senior signal is connecting it to real kernel behaviour and tuning.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: When RAM is full the kernel must evict a page, writing it out first if dirty. OPT evicts the page used furthest in the future: optimal but impossible, only a benchmark. FIFO is simple but can fault more with more frames (Belady's anomaly). LRU is good but exact tracking is too expensive per access, so systems use Clock, an approximation: pages sit in a circle with an accessed bit, and the hand clears bits until it finds a page with 0. Linux keeps active and inactive lists for file and anonymous pages, and kswapd reclaims in the background.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Clock: [A:1][B:0][C:1][D:1]  hand->B: bit 0 => evict B
                  hand passes A,C... clearing bits (second chance)

The hardware sets the accessed bit in the PTE on every access, which gives the OS a cheap signal without trapping each access.

Linux specifics:

  • Active/inactive LRU lists; a page is promoted when referenced twice. Newer kernels (6.1+) have MGLRU (multi-generational LRU).
  • kswapd wakes below the low watermark; if free memory hits the min watermark, allocating processes do direct reclaim and stall.
  • Clean file pages are dropped for free; anonymous pages need swap; dirty file pages are written back first.
  • vm.swappiness (0-100, default 60) biases between swapping anonymous pages and dropping file cache.

Known bad case: a looping sequential scan larger than RAM defeats LRU (each page is evicted right before reuse). Databases use scan-resistant policies (2Q, LRU-K, clock-pro).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying LRU is optimal; OPT is.
  • Treating low free as pressure; Linux fills spare RAM with cache. Look at available.
  • Believing swappiness 0 disables swap.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is Belady's anomaly? -> FIFO with 4 frames can fault more than with 3 on some reference strings.
  2. Why is exact LRU impractical? -> It needs a timestamp or list update on every memory access.
  3. What does direct reclaim mean for latency? -> The allocating thread itself does the freeing work, producing latency spikes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: lists FIFO/LRU/OPT. Senior knows Clock, the accessed bit, Linux lists/watermarks/MGLRU, scan-resistance and how this shows in vmstat and PSI.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A nightly full-table scan evicted a database's hot pages from the OS cache; the team moved the scan to a replica and used posix_fadvise(DONTNEED).

questions.contextHtml:
A PostgreSQL primary (64 GB RAM) runs shared_buffers = 32GB and max_connections = 400, with typically 350 active. The kernel memory looks wrong:

$ grep -E 'PageTables|MemAvailable|Hugepage' /proc/meminfo
MemAvailable:   11200000 kB
PageTables:     21500000 kB
Hugepagesize:       2048 kB
HugePages_Total:        0
$ grep VmPTE /proc/$(pgrep -f 'postgres: app' | head -1)/status
VmPTE:     61000 kB
$ cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
always [madvise] never

The box occasionally gets OOM-killed under connection spikes. The team wants to move to a 128 GB instance.
questions.promptHtml: Explain where the memory went and propose a cheaper fix, including how to roll it out safely.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Upgrade the instance" or "reduce shared_buffers", without noticing page tables are 21 GB.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Postgres version (huge_pages setting support)? Is the host dedicated? Can we afford a restart window? Do we run in a container with a memory limit?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap connections via PgBouncer (400 backends to about 80) to cut page-table and per-backend memory immediately.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) per-process page tables for the shared buffer mapping: each backend maps 32 GB with 4 KB pages; (b) work_mem blowups; (c) a leak. PageTables of 21 GB against VmPTE of 61 MB x 350 backends matches (a).
  4. How I'd verify: The arithmetic: 32 GB / 4 KB = 8.4 M PTEs x 8 B = 64 MB per backend; 350 x 61 MB is about 21 GB. Confirm HugePages_Total: 0.
  5. Root cause: Every backend touching the shared buffers builds its own page table for the same physical pages. With 4 KB pages this is 64 MB per backend; 350 backends waste ~21 GB of RAM, which then looks like memory pressure and OOM kills on spikes.
  6. Fix: Enable explicit huge pages: reserve vm.nr_hugepages slightly above shared memory size (about 32 GB / 2 MB = 16,384, plus margin to about 16,900), set huge_pages = on in Postgres (use try first), then restart. Page tables drop about 512x, to roughly 40 MB in total.
# size from Postgres itself (PG 15+): 
postgres -D $PGDATA -C shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages
sysctl -w vm.nr_hugepages=16900
echo 'vm.nr_hugepages=16900' >> /etc/sysctl.d/90-hugepages.conf

Roll out on a replica first, measure PageTables, restart primary in a window, fail over if needed. 7. Prevention: Dashboard PageTables and HugePages_Free; capacity doc formula; connection pooling policy. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Huge pages are reserved and unavailable to other uses; reserve too many and the OS starves, too few and Postgres with huge_pages = on refuses to start (so try first). I would not rely on THP for this, as madvise mode will not cover shared memory and always risks latency spikes. And not buy a 2x instance for a 21 GB accounting issue.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does it help the TLB? -> Yes, fewer misses on the buffer pool as a side benefit.
  • Can you resize the reservation online? -> nr_hugepages can grow if contiguous memory exists; may fail on fragmented hosts, so reserve at boot.
  • Containers? -> Hugepages are a separate resource in Kubernetes with explicit requests.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 'memory-hungry Postgres' upgrade request was cancelled when someone divided PageTables by backend count; huge pages gave back about a third of the machine.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests bigger instance or lower buffers.
  • Hire: Finds the page-table overhead and enables huge pages.
  • Strong hire: Does the math, sizes nr_hugepages, plans staged rollout, and discusses pooling and trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml:
A Redis cluster (r6 instances, 64 GB, 20 GB dataset) shows p99 latency of 2 ms, but every few minutes some commands stall 300-900 ms. CPU is low, network is fine. After the AMI was updated last week, spikes appeared.

$ redis-cli --intrinsic-latency 60
Max latency so far: 872 microseconds   (host is healthy)
$ redis-cli latency doctor
fork: 3 events; latency 410 ms ...
$ cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
[always] madvise never
$ grep -E 'thp_fault_alloc|thp_collapse|compact_stall' /proc/vmstat
compact_stall 18211
thp_collapse_alloc 9920
$ grep AnonHugePages /proc/meminfo
AnonHugePages:  21000000 kB

BGSAVE runs hourly. The spikes also occur between saves. Someone suspects the network; someone wants to add replicas.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames network or adds replicas; does not connect the AMI change and THP.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What exactly changed in the AMI (THP default)? Do the stalls correlate with BGSAVE/AOF rewrite? What does latency history say per event type? Any swap?
  2. Immediate mitigation: echo madvise > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled (or never) and defrag set to madvise; this takes effect for new allocations immediately, and restart/failover replicas for existing mappings. Roll node by node via failover.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) THP enabled=always causing compaction stalls and khugepaged work (compact_stall 18k); (b) fork + COW with huge pages (copying 2 MB per write instead of 4 KB); (c) swapping; (d) network jitter. latency doctor pointing at fork and the AMI timeline favour (a)/(b).
  4. How I'd verify: /proc/vmstat deltas for compact_stall, thp_* during a spike; perf trace/perf top for compact_zone; redis-cli info stats latest_fork_usec; compare A/B by disabling THP on one replica.
  5. Root cause: With always, the kernel promotes ranges into 2 MB pages and may stall allocations to compact memory (direct compaction). During BGSAVE the child shares pages copy-on-write; one small write by Redis now copies a whole 2 MB page, causing big latency and memory bloat (a 20 GB dataset can nearly double). Redis documents this advice: disable THP.
  6. Fix: Set THP to madvise/never persistently (kernel cmdline transparent_hugepage=madvise or a systemd unit), keep the AMI baseline pinned, and check latest_fork_usec.
echo madvise > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
echo madvise > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/defrag
  1. Prevention: AMI baseline test comparing p99 and THP settings; alert on compact_stall rate and fork time; Redis warns about THP at startup, so make it fail CI.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Disabling THP raises TLB misses slightly; for a 20 GB dataset on Redis that is usually the better trade. I would not add replicas (spreads the symptom), and would not disable THP only on the master without checking replicas that may promote.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would explicit huge pages be an alternative? -> Predictable and not compacted at runtime, but Redis does not use hugetlbfs by default.
  • Why does fork itself take long? -> Copying page tables; 20 GB is about 40 MB of PTEs (verify latest_fork_usec), and slower on some virtualisation (Xen) setups.
  • Why do spikes happen between saves? -> khugepaged collapse and direct compaction run independently of fork.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fleet rebuilt on a new base image showed a 5x p99 regression across all Redis nodes; the diff of /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled between old and new images was the whole root cause.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suspects network or scales out.
  • Hire: Identifies THP and sets madvise/never.
  • Strong hire: Explains COW amplification with fork, compaction stalls, verifies with vmstat counters, and plans rolling changes with baseline tests.

questions.contextHtml:
A 64-core ingest service (C++) memory-maps and unmaps 8 MB buffers per request across 48 worker threads. Throughput stops scaling at about 16 threads and adding cores makes it slower. CPU profile:

$ perf top -g
  22.1%  [kernel]  smp_call_function_many_cond
  14.0%  [kernel]  flush_tlb_mm_range
  11.3%  [kernel]  unmap_page_range
$ grep TLB /proc/interrupts | head -2
TLB:  8812334  9120011  9023009 ...   TLB shootdowns   (per CPU, +1.3M/s)
$ perf stat -e dTLB-load-misses ./svc   # moderate

Disk, network and locks (perf lock) look fine. The service allocates buffers with mmap/munmap each request. Someone proposes pinning threads to cores and upgrading the NIC.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Lock contention" or "NIC", guessing without reading kernel symbols; no explanation of why more threads make it worse.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do all threads share one address space (yes, threads)? How often is munmap called per second? Is memory reused? Which allocator?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap workers at the knee (about 16) for now so we do not waste cores, then reduce munmap frequency by pooling buffers.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) TLB shootdown storm from frequent munmap/mprotect in a multithreaded process; (b) mmap_lock contention; (c) page-fault cost; (d) NUMA remote access. Symbols flush_tlb_mm_range, smp_call_function_many_cond and TLB interrupts at 1.3M/s name (a).
  4. How I'd verify: perf top/perf record -g; sample /proc/interrupts TLB line over 10 s; strace -c -f -e trace=mmap,munmap for call rates; compare with a pooled-buffer prototype and perf stat.
  5. Root cause: Unmapping or changing permissions of memory in a shared address space requires removing stale translations from every core that ran any thread of the process. The kernel sends an IPI to each of those cores and waits. With 48 threads on 48 cores every munmap interrupts up to 47 other cores, so the cost scales with core count, and cores spend time handling IPIs rather than working.
  6. Fix: Allocate once and reuse: a buffer pool or arena recycled per request; or use jemalloc/tcmalloc with retained memory; avoid MADV_DONTNEED churn too; batch frees. If isolation is needed, shard into processes (separate address spaces) per core group.
// reuse, don't unmap: keep a lock-free freelist of 8 MB buffers
Buf* b = pool.acquire();   // mmap only if pool empty
handle(*b);
pool.release(b);           // no munmap on the hot path
  1. Prevention: Track TLB interrupts rate and munmap calls/s in perf regression tests; code review rule against per-request mmap/munmap in threaded services; scalability test at full core count.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Pooling holds memory longer (higher steady RSS; bound the pool and trim periodically). Not core pinning or NIC upgrades, which do not touch the cause. Not vm.max_map_count tweaks.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does Java rarely show this? -> The GC manages one big mapping and rarely unmaps.
  • Does PCID help? -> It reduces flushes on context switch, not cross-CPU shootdowns.
  • What if threads are pinned to few cores? -> Shootdowns only target CPUs in the mm's cpumask, so fewer cores means fewer IPIs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 'perfectly parallel' image pipeline got slower beyond 12 cores; the cure was a free-list of buffers and a deleted munmap, doubling throughput at 64 cores.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Guesses locks/NIC.
  • Hire: Reads perf symbols, identifies TLB shootdown and removes munmap churn.
  • Strong hire: Explains IPI mechanics and scaling, quantifies via interrupts, bounds the pool and offers process-sharding alternative.

questions.promptHtml: When would you use explicit hugetlbfs huge pages versus Transparent Huge Pages, and what are the failure modes of each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Looks for judgment on a high-impact tuning knob where wrong choices cause outages.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Huge pages (2 MB, or 1 GB) cut TLB misses and page-table size. Explicit hugetlbfs pages are reserved up front, never swapped, and predictable, so I use them for large fixed shared memory like a database buffer pool or DPDK. THP is automatic (kernel and khugepaged merge ranges), convenient but can cause latency spikes from compaction, memory bloat and large COW copies, so latency-sensitive stores like Redis and MongoDB recommend madvise or never.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Explicit (hugetlbfs) THP
Setup vm.nr_hugepages, app opts in (MAP_HUGETLB, huge_pages=on) enabled: always/madvise/never
Predictability High Variable
Swappable No (reserved) Split then swapped
Failure Reservation too small: app fails or falls back; too large: starves OS Compaction stalls, bloat, COW amplification
Typical use Postgres, Oracle, JVM -XX:+UseLargePages, DPDK General apps, JVM -XX:+UseTransparentHugePages opt-in

Why larger pages help: TLB reach goes from 6 MB (1,536 x 4 KB) to 3 GB (1,536 x 2 MB); page tables shrink 512x. Why they hurt: allocation needs physically contiguous 2 MB, which fragmentation can make unavailable; internal fragmentation wastes memory for sparse touches; one dirty byte copies 2 MB on COW.

grep -i huge /proc/meminfo
cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/{enabled,defrag}
grep -E 'thp_|compact_' /proc/vmstat

Recommended practice: THP madvise globally, explicit huge pages for big known mappings, measure tail latency, never flip fleet-wide untested.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Enabling THP everywhere because it "improves performance" without checking p99.
  • Reserving huge pages after the system has been up a while (fragmentation can make reservation fail); reserve at boot.
  • Expecting normal allocations to use reserved huge pages; they cannot.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does defrag=always do? -> Direct compaction on fault, which stalls the allocating thread.
  2. How do you size nr_hugepages? -> Segment size / 2 MB plus margin; Postgres can print the exact need.
  3. 1 GB pages? -> Used for very large, long-lived mappings (DPDK, VMs); must be reserved at boot.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "huge pages make things faster". Senior states the mechanism (TLB reach, PTE size), both modes' failure modes, workload guidance and a measure-first rollout.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fleet-wide THP=always rollout cut CPU 4% on batch services and tripled p99 on a cache tier within an hour; rollback was a sysfs write, but the lesson was per-tier policy.

questions.contextHtml:
You are consolidating two services onto shared 32 GB nodes in Kubernetes to save cost: a latency-sensitive API (p99 target 50 ms, 8 GB working set) and a batch exporter that reads large files and writes 3-4 GB of output per run. You migrate 10% of API traffic to a consolidated node and see 150 ms stalls during exporter runs, with no CPU contention.

$ vmstat 1 (during export)
 r b  swpd  free   buff  cache    si so    bi     bo
 2 1     0 112000  4000 21000000  0  0  120000  95000
$ cat /proc/pressure/memory
some avg10=18.40 full avg10=6.20
$ grep -E 'allocstall|pgscan_direct|pgsteal_direct' /proc/vmstat
allocstall_normal 48210
pgscan_direct 9120000
$ sysctl vm.min_free_kbytes vm.dirty_ratio
vm.min_free_kbytes = 67584
vm.dirty_ratio = 20

Swap is disabled, no OOM kills. The exporter writes through the page cache and uses a lot of readahead.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the stalls and propose a plan to proceed with the consolidation safely.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Not enough RAM, buy more", or "set swappiness to 0" without understanding direct reclaim.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the exporter share a cgroup with the API? Are cgroup memory limits set for each? What storage serves the exporter? Is traffic shift reversible quickly?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause the migration (revert the 10%), throttle or reschedule the exporter, and keep the API node pool separate until fixed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the exporter fills the page cache with dirty and clean pages, keeping free memory near the min watermark, so the API's allocations hit direct reclaim (allocstall 48k); (b) dirty throttling at dirty_ratio; (c) CPU throttling; (d) swap thrash (ruled out, no swap).
  4. How I'd verify: allocstall_* and pgscan_direct deltas correlate with exporter runs; grep Dirty /proc/meminfo; PSI some/full; perf trace-style analysis of API threads in shrink_node; try the exporter with posix_fadvise(DONTNEED) or systemd-run -p MemoryHigh in a test.
  5. Root cause: The exporter's streaming I/O consumes nearly all free memory as page cache. When the API allocates, kswapd is not fast enough and the API's own thread must reclaim pages directly (scanning lists, possibly waiting for writeback), which shows up as 100+ ms stalls. Clean cache is cheap to drop but dirty cache requires I/O.
  6. Fix: Give each workload its own cgroup limits and use memory.high on the exporter so it is throttled and reclaimed before it pressures the node; have the exporter use O_DIRECT or fadvise(DONTNEED)/periodic sync_file_range so the cache does not balloon; lower dirty_background_bytes for smoother write-back; consider raising vm.min_free_kbytes modestly and watermark_scale_factor so kswapd starts earlier. Schedule the exporter off-peak.
# exporter slice: throttle before it can starve neighbours
systemd-run --slice=batch -p MemoryHigh=6G -p MemoryMax=8G -p IOWeight=50 ./exporter
  1. Prevention: Per-service PSI dashboards and alerts on allocstall; canary rollout with a performance gate (p99); resource isolation requirement for co-location.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: memory.high slows the exporter (fine for batch). Raising min_free_kbytes wastes RAM. I would not co-locate without isolation to save cost; I would not drop caches in a cron job.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not swappiness=0? -> There is no swap anyway; the pressure is cache, not anonymous memory.
  • Would a bigger node fix it? -> Delays it: the cache grows to fill any size; isolation fixes it.
  • NUMA effects? -> Per-node reclaim can start while the other node has free memory; check numastat.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cost-saving consolidation passed all CPU tests and failed on page cache. The batch job was the noisy neighbour, found only by correlating allocstall with its start times.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Wants more RAM or random sysctl changes.
  • Hire: Explains direct reclaim from cache pressure and isolates the exporter.
  • Strong hire: Uses cgroup memory.high, fadvise/O_DIRECT, watermark/dirty tuning, canary gates and quantified verification.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review. A Java service using a JNI image library crashed 14 times across a week, each time the container vanished and restarted. App logs end abruptly; no OutOfMemoryError. Kubernetes showed exit code 134 on two of the restarts and 139 on the rest. The node's dmesg:

java[4410]: segfault at 10 ip 00007f1a2c3b4a12 sp 00007f1a1d7fe8f0 error 4 in libimgproc.so[7f1a2c390000+4e000]

A hs_err_pid4410.log file was found in the container's working dir on one occasion, but the pod filesystem was ephemeral so most were lost. The first responder restarted pods and closed the ticket as "Java flakiness".
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: what happened, what evidence was missing, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase heap" or "Java is flaky"; no handle on exit codes, native vs managed, or evidence capture.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which input triggered each crash? Is the library version recent? Are core dumps and hs_err files persisted? Does the crash correlate with certain image types or concurrency?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pin or roll back the library version, run the risky decode in an out-of-process worker (so a crash kills a helper, not the service), and add retries on the client side.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) invalid memory access in native code: segfault at 10 = null pointer plus offset 0x10 inside libimgproc.so; (b) JNI misuse (using a freed handle after the Java object was GC'd, passing a closed buffer); (c) OOM kill (rule out, no kill message); (d) JVM bug. Exit 139 = 128 + 11 (SIGSEGV), 134 = 128 + 6 (SIGABRT, JVM fatal error abort).
  4. How I'd verify: dmesg fault address and ip offset: addr2line/objdump -d with the library at 0x…a12 - base; the hs_err log's "Problematic frame: C [libimgproc.so+0x...]" and Java stack; enable core dumps with a persistent volume; reproduce under valgrind/ASan build of the library with the captured input.
  5. Root cause (as established): A null dereference at offset 0x10 in native code, typically a struct field read through a null pointer, triggered by malformed or edge-case images (library returned NULL on decode failure, the wrapper ignored it). Java code cannot segfault by itself, so a managed exception was not available to catch it: the whole JVM dies, and every in-flight request with it. The review's real failure was process: no evidence retained, symptom closed as flakiness.
  6. Fix: Short term: validate inputs, check return codes in the JNI wrapper, upgrade the library, isolate in a sandbox process. Long term: fuzz the decoder, add -XX:ErrorFile=/persistent/hs_err_%p.log and -XX:+CreateCoredumpOnCrash, persistent crash volume, symbolised stack collection.
# JVM flags: keep crash evidence
-XX:ErrorFile=/var/crash/hs_err_%p.log -XX:+CreateCoredumpOnCrash
kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.exitCode}'
  1. Prevention: Alert on any exit code 134/139/137 restarts; crash-loop runbook; native dependency review and ASan test builds; image fuzzing in CI.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Out-of-process isolation adds latency and complexity but contains blast radius. Not a global catch Throwable (it cannot catch a segfault). Not increasing heap or restarting more often.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How do you tell native OOM from segfault? -> dmesg shows 'Out of memory: Killed process' and exit code 137 versus 'segfault at'.
  • Why a SIGABRT in 2 cases? -> JVM detected the fatal error and aborted after writing hs_err, or native code called abort().
  • Can you run ASan in production? -> Costly (~2x slowdown and more memory); use on a canary slice.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A weekly 'JVM flakiness' turned out to be one customer's TIFF files hitting an unchecked NULL in a decoder. The crash had been in the logs for months; no one had read the exit code.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames the JVM or heap; no evidence-gathering plan.
  • Hire: Reads the exit codes and dmesg, identifies native null dereference, proposes isolation and library fix.
  • Strong hire: Adds crash-evidence retention, addr2line symbolisation, fuzzing and alerting policy.
